1.pericope_label: The priests, the captain of the temple and the Sadducees come upon them, grieved that they preached the resurrection

schools.summary: Calvin allows the arrest a show of law which only its outcome exposes, and reckons the infamy that private men incur in taking up a public charge; Gill supplies that John preached as well as Peter.
Henry turns the opposition into a rule of resolution for Christ’s servants.

Robertson and Lightfoot identify the captain from Jewish and rabbinic sources; Ellicott describes his nightly rounds and traces the Sadducees’ vindictiveness to their earlier defeat, noting that in Acts they and not the Pharisees are the persecutors; Barnes takes the party for peace officers rather than a mob and locates the offence as much in the teachers as in the doctrine.

Clarke grounds the anger in the Sadducean denial of immortality and any future world; Wesley finds it in their own guilt for the crucifixion, and reads the arrest as God’s ordering that they testify first in the temple and then before the council.
Chrysostom reads the choice of officer as a design to give a private grievance the colour of public criminality.

debates.question: Did the party come as magistrates or as a mob?

sides.position: As keepers of the peace expecting a tumult, though the verb still implies suddenness
Of set purpose, with a genuine show of law that only the outcome exposes as wicked
By design, to dress a private grievance as a public crime

debates.question: Why did the preaching grieve them?

sides.position: Because the Sadducean denial of immortality and a future world was at stake
Because their authority was bypassed by unauthorised teachers, the miracle itself never being examined
Because the resurrection convicted them of the crucifixion
Because old defeat had added vindictiveness to a calculating policy

3.pericope_label: They are put in hold until the morrow, and the number of believers reaches about five thousand

schools.summary: Gill notes the version that has both apostles seized by force; Calvin takes the number for the whole church and marvels that unarmed men without garrisons show more power in their voice than the world does in raging, and that novices were not discouraged from taking up the cross at so hard a beginning.
Henry states that the church’s suffering days have sometimes been her growing days.

Barnes explains the custody and the hour and reads the growth as the standing proof that persecution spreads what it means to destroy, taking the number as a running total; Robertson locates the ward and notes that the delay observed a rule broken at Christ’s own trial; Ellicott fixes the times, renders the figure as a total made up to five thousand, and draws the parallel with the feeding of the five thousand.
Clarke itemises the arithmetic of the five thousand, denies that all were converted that day, and calls the result a goodly flock as the church’s commencement.

debates.question: Does the five thousand count that day’s converts or the whole body?

sides.position: The whole body to date, since so many could not have been converted at one portico
The whole body, itemised: a hundred and twenty, three thousand, and one thousand eight hundred and eighty since

debates.question: Why record the growth at the moment of the arrest?

sides.position: Because persecution is the very means by which doctrines spread
Because the church’s suffering days have sometimes been her growing days

5.pericope_label: On the morrow the rulers, elders and scribes are gathered together at Jerusalem

schools.summary: Calvin sees only tyranny restrained by fear of the people, and raises the chronological difficulty about which man held the high priesthood; Gill notes the overnight custody.
Henry finds a slackening in the daylight sitting, weighs the learning and power ranged against the gospel, and counts Jerusalem itself an aggravation.

Robertson gives the three classes and numbers of the Sanhedrin; Barnes glosses the elders, catches the Gentile-facing their rulers, and infers from the council’s wanderings why the trial was deferred; Ellicott repunctuates the verse and dates the sitting as the first formal one since Christ’s trial; Lightfoot weighs both senses of at Jerusalem and doubts the arrest was made by a proper Sanhedrim at all.
Clarke identifies the assembly as the grand council; Wesley marks the judges as eminent for power, wisdom and learning.

debates.question: Why were they gathered, and what does at Jerusalem indicate?

sides.position: Summoned expressly to meet the new facts, the first formal sitting since Christ’s trial
Probably in the city for a solemnity of the day rather than for this case
Named because the council by then sometimes sat elsewhere; the members were absent the night before

debates.question: How eager was the court?

sides.position: Less hot than at Christ’s trial, since they waited for daylight; it was well if they began to relent
As tyrannous as they dared be, and restrained only by fear of the people

6.pericope_label: Annas, Caiaphas, John and Alexander gathered; by what power or by what name have ye done this?

schools.summary: Gill allows the title either from past office or from the deputyship but denies the presidency, and describes the half-circle of the court; Calvin allows the judges a feigned zeal for God’s glory while they labour to wring a denial out of the apostles by fear.

Robertson separates the Roman legal title from the Jewish opinion and hears a magical formula behind the question; Ellicott supplies the dates, proposes the presidency as the reason for the title, gives the rabbi’s death-bed words, and hears scorn in the refusal to call the cure a sign; Barnes knows nothing of the minor names and reads the question as intimidation that never examines the miracle; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic identification and the tradition of the opening temple gates.

Clarke accounts for the retained title from the length of the tenure and the five sons who succeeded, adopts the rabbinic identification of the third name, and reads the question as a legal trap for a capital charge of magic; Wesley states the bare succession and calls the question deliberately ambiguous.

debates.question: Why is Annas called the high priest?

sides.position: He had held the office eleven years and bore the title for life
Caiaphas held it by Roman law, Annas in the opinion of the Jews
He probably presided over this very council as its President
From past office or the deputyship, but not from any presidency, which Gamaliel then held

debates.question: What is the force of the question put to them?

sides.position: A trap: a suspicion of magic that might carry a capital charge
Scorn: they concede the cure but refuse to name it a sign
Intimidation, assuming imposture without ever examining the miracle
A feigned zeal for God’s honour, meant to frighten them into a denial

8.pericope_label: Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost, answers the rulers concerning the good deed done to the impotent man

schools.summary: Calvin grounds the boldness wholly in the Spirit, since the man who quailed before a servant girl would have fainted at their pomp, and hears a taunting preface in the appeal to a good deed; Gill dates the filling to the instant and marks the alteration in the man.

Barnes reads the boldness as proof of a genuine repentance seeking to repair the evil done in that very room, and finds the address wholly respectful; Ellicott makes the tense a sudden inspiration, notes the matching names on the two sides of the chamber, traces more deference here than in Paul’s later address, and glosses the good deed and the pregnant verb for healing; Robertson calls the substitution of benefactor for malefactor a skilful turn.
Clarke sees the promise of unpremeditated speech fulfilled; Wesley makes the timing the point, that God moves his instruments when he sees it needful, and notes the honour paid to the office.
Cyril of Jerusalem sets the hour in a longer arc of one Spirit working from Pentecost through the healing at the Beautiful gate to the confuting of the rulers.

debates.question: What accounts for Peter’s boldness?

sides.position: The Spirit alone; of himself he would have fainted at their pomp
A genuine repentance seeking to undo the denial made before these very men
A sudden inspiration given at the moment it was needed

debates.question: In what tone does he begin?

sides.position: With perfect respect, not questioning the court’s authority
With more deference than Paul would later show the same court
With a taunting preface, girding judges who sit to condemn good deeds

10.pericope_label: By the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom ye crucified: this is the stone set at nought of you builders

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the subterfuges were refused, orders the argument from miracle to resurrection, and turns the rejected stone into a standing check on ecclesiastical office, the papacy included; Gill identifies the stone with the Messiah.

Barnes calls the avowal the greatest instance of boldness and argues that only the truth of the religion accounts for the change in Peter; Robertson marks the emphatic pronoun and the play on words and leaves the corner stone’s position open; Ellicott fixes the responsibility on the council rather than Pilate and reads the builders as their own official calling; Lightfoot sets out why the Jews would never apply the verse to their Messiah.

Clarke rests on the plain evidence of the cure and infers that the rest of the prophecy will be fulfilled as literally as the rejection was; Wesley observes that the council never dared plead before the apostles the tale they had paid the soldiers to tell.

debates.question: To whom did the Jews apply the stone?

sides.position: To Jacob, or David, or the congregation of Israel, but never to their Messiah
To David, on the ancient reading; the apostles apply it without doubt to the Messiah
To David truly, but as a shadow of what God expressed perfectly in the Messiah
They had heard it applied already and thought in their blindness they could defy the warning

debates.question: Who is charged with the crucifixion?

sides.position: The council itself, whatever the formal sentence Pilate gave
They are charged so that they may know they strove against God in vain, not merely to upbraid them
They knew it in conscience, and never dared plead their bought story

12.pericope_label: Neither is there salvation in any other, for there is none other name whereby we must be saved

schools.summary: Calvin makes the miracle a token that Christ is the only author of life, hears a sting for the priests who tried to blot out the name, grounds the exclusiveness in the decree, and explains that God reached out his hand because men cannot ascend to him; Gill enumerates what salvation is not in.

Barnes traces the word for salvation and gives two reasons for the turn from the cure to the doctrine; Ellicott finds the earlier verb reaching its highest sense and extends the Name to cover the heathen who never heard it; Robertson refuses any such extension and applies the exclusive clause to the modern mission field by name.

Wesley calls the movement a beautiful gradation after the custom of Christ himself; Clarke allows no other person, no other name, and no other means, all earlier means being subordinate to the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

debates.question: How far does the exclusive Name reach?

sides.position: Beyond those who hear it; the heathen who are saved are saved by a Name they never heard
Not at all beyond it; there is no second name to set beside it anywhere on earth
It is exclusive because God decreed it so, and will not make salvation common by any other means

debates.question: Why does Peter turn from the cure to salvation?

sides.position: The temporal deliverance suggested the greater, and the occasion offered the council a doctrine they already professed
By a deliberate gradation, after his Master’s habit of rising from earthly things to spiritual
Because the miracle was given to show Christ the only author of life

13.pericope_label: They marvel at the boldness of unlearned men, take knowledge that they had been with Jesus, and can say nothing against the healed man

schools.summary: Calvin turns the recognition into self-conviction, since to confess the sign manifest is to condemn oneself, and asks whether the arm of God is broken when two simple men are silenced; Gill has the healed man appearing of his own accord as a witness.

Robertson defines both words as marks of standing rather than capacity and notes that Peter had arraigned the court before God; Ellicott derives the first from the scribes’ own name and traces the second into the modern word idiot, and observes that John’s bearing spoke though he did not; Barnes keeps the older sense, supposes the recognition came from the miracle and the boldness, and calls the healed man’s presence unanswerable.
Clarke rejects the English rendering of ignorant outright and credits the apostles with strong common sense; Wesley draws the general rule that God has in all ages used such men to preach.

debates.question: What do unlearned and ignorant mean?

sides.position: Not educated as a scribe, and a common man — the word that later became idiot
Without rabbinical training, and a layman rather than an officer
The English rendering is improper; in no sense were the apostles ignorant men
Men without education or practice in public speaking, and Galileans besides

debates.question: How did the council know they had been with Jesus?

sides.position: They began to recognise their faces from the temple teaching
It is not said; probably from the miracle, the boldness, and what such boldness implied
By an unwilling wonder that convicted their own consciences

15.pericope_label: The council confers apart: what shall we do to these men, for a notable miracle is manifest and we cannot deny it

schools.summary: Gill enumerates the penalties weighed and suggests the healed man withdrew with the apostles.
Henry answers their question with what they should have done, explains why the prisoners were sent out, and reads the trial as a graded schooling in suffering.

Robertson has the court comparing notes on its predicament and reduces the admission to calculation; Barnes lists the penalties considered, explains why a threat was thought sufficient and notes that it failed; Ellicott objects that a court of justice had abandoned its office for a debate on expediency and hears a frustrated will in the confession.
Clarke sets out the public evidence that made denial impossible.

debates.question: What was the court actually deciding?

sides.position: Which penalty would stop the preaching, fear of the people ruling out the severer ones
Nothing it had any business deciding; a court of justice had turned to a debate on policy
A question that answers itself, if they would receive the doctrine and be baptized

debates.question: What does we cannot deny it reveal?

sides.position: A will to deny that lacks the power
A calculation that denial would do no good with the man standing there
A fact so public that no means of disproof existed

17.pericope_label: Let us straitly threaten them, and they command them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus

schools.summary: Gill limits the fear to the country beyond Jerusalem; Calvin draws from the command a rule that pastoral authority has bounds it may not pass, beyond which obedience may lawfully be refused, and warns against preferring the wicked to church government.

Lightfoot contrasts their tolerance of the Baptist and infers that they knew or suspected Jesus was the Messiah; Ellicott identifies the reduplicated idiom and weighs whether it proves an Aramaic original; Barnes glosses the Hebraism; Robertson marks the contemptuous this name and the grammar of the command.

Clarke identifies what they feared, reckons the converts already made, traces the hatred to their own guilt as crucifiers, and makes the unpopularity of the doctrine an argument for its truth; Wesley calls their view of the gospel a gangrene, divides speaking from teaching, and tells the court it does nothing.

debates.question: Why so implacable against this name in particular?

sides.position: Because they knew, or suspected, that he was the Messiah; they had tolerated the Baptist
Because they were his crucifiers and could not bear salvation preached through him
Their recoil shows in the wording: they slur at this name rather than speak it

debates.question: Does the reduplicated threat point to an Aramaic original?

sides.position: So far as it goes yes, though a Greek speaker might have reproduced the old formula
Yes; it proves the council’s words were translated just as spoken
It is simply a Hebraism of intensity, and the grammar needs no more explanation

19.pericope_label: Whether it be right to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye: we cannot but speak

schools.summary: Calvin denies obedience to pastors who abuse a real authority, subjects all their traditions to the rule of the Word, and yet cautions that much may rightly be concealed for peace, the gospel alone being exempt; Gill distinguishes moral from physical impossibility.

Barnes reads the verse as an early charter of liberty of conscience and shows why the court could not resist the appeal; Ellicott grants the axiom but limits it by the difference between witnessing to facts and proclaiming opinions, and places the burden of proof on whoever claims the higher authority; Robertson calls the defiance justified and the courage that of martyrs in every age.
Clarke opposes secular prudence to acting before God and calls suppression of the testimony treason; Wesley sets a pagan philosopher’s answer to his judges beside the apostles’.

debates.question: How far does the right of conscience extend?

sides.position: Responsibility for religious opinion is direct to God, and no man may control it
Even to lawful church authority, which forfeits obedience the moment it leads away from God
Axiomatic for witness to facts, but narrowing as one passes to doctrine, opinion and conjecture
To justified defiance, where authority steps between the conscience and God

debates.question: Why could they not be silent?

sides.position: A necessity was laid on them by the evidence and by the command to preach
Because it is the gospel that is in hand; other things may rightly be concealed for peace
Because suppressing the testimony would be treason against God

21.pericope_label: They threaten them further and let them go, for all men glorified God, the man being above forty years old

schools.summary: Calvin looks past the human cause to the providence that binds the wicked without their knowledge, finds the adversaries confirming the gospel against their will, insists the victory is still under the cross, and doubts that all who praised God came the whole way to Christ; Gill supposes the threats were repeated or sharpened for want of an answer.

Barnes traces the release to fear of a tumult and reads the popular praise as the highest evidence of the miracle; Robertson finds irony in the continued glorifying while the council still threatened; Ellicott notes the same tense and the writer’s habit of recording the impression made on the people and the duration of infirmities.

Clarke counts the converts that made an insurrection likely, reports a variant reading of the clause, and turns the man’s forty years into an argument that no age is beyond conversion but none may presume on it; Wesley finds the people wiser than their rulers.

debates.question: Why did the council stop at threats?

sides.position: It could punish no further without a tumult, its power depending on the people’s caprice
The converts were by now numerous enough to make an insurrection likely
Regard of the people restrained them, but it was God who bound them, unknown to themselves

debates.question: What does the people’s glorifying prove?

sides.position: The reality of the miracle, since neither adversaries nor neighbours questioned it
The helplessness of the court, praised over while it was still threatening
Real fruit, but perhaps not saving fruit; to feel the power and not come to Christ is to stop midway

23.pericope_label: Being let go, they went to their own company and reported all that the chief priests and elders had said

schools.summary: Calvin gives emboldening and prayer as the two ends and insists that the apostles never submitted servilely to the decree; Gill notes the dismissal from custody.

Henry draws two lessons from the return, that honour should not lift a man above the communion of saints and that a public station must seek the public good, and adds that the record was kept for posterity.

Ellicott infers a recognised place of meeting and widens the chief priests to the heads of the courses; Robertson takes the company as the whole brotherhood and finds real apprehension behind the report; Barnes reads the report as a consultation about whether to obey or to leave the city.
Clarke identifies this as the first persecution since the resurrection and pictures the church already at prayer when the two arrived.

Chrysostom denies any motive of glory in the telling, notes that they reported the adversaries’ words and omitted their own, and admires the fitness with which each apostolic prayer addresses the attribute the occasion needs.

debates.question: Why did they report what was said?

sides.position: Not for their own glory but to display the proofs of Christ’s grace, omitting their own part
To embolden the brethren and to arm them with prayer against the threatenings
To take counsel about what they should now do, a proper example under persecution
Because for all the defiance they had real apprehension of the outcome

debates.question: What was their own company?

sides.position: A recognised society meeting at fixed times in a known place
The whole body of disciples, not the apostles only
The church already gathered in supplication for their safety
The fellowship whose duties and privileges no honour puts a man above

24.pericope_label: They lifted up their voice with one accord: Lord, thou art God, who by the mouth of thy servant David hast said

schools.summary: Gill reports the Jewish tradition of the Psalm’s authorship and its messianic reading; Calvin insists that David speaks first of himself and his own hard-won kingdom, which was established to be a figure, so that he does not stay in the shadow but apprehends the body, and draws from the prayer the rule that God’s power and promise are the two foundations of boldness.

Ellicott weighs three accounts of the joint utterance and prefers that the people followed Peter clause by clause, calls the prayer the church’s earliest recorded praise, and treats the citation as a lesson in apostolic interpretation; Barnes glosses the Hebrew idiom, the unbroken union of the company and the force of the title, and holds the Psalm to speak solely of the Messiah; Robertson reports the suggestion that the company sang the Psalm and glosses the verb for raging.
Clarke paraphrases the title as universal rule and unlimited power; Wesley compresses the whole prayer into a sentence.

debates.question: Of whom does the second Psalm speak?

sides.position: Directly and solely of the Messiah; the apostles’ use settles it
Of David first and truly, but as a figure whose body is Christ
Of the Messiah, by the settled sense of the ancient doctors, though some read it of Gog and Magog
Of Christ, predicting the vain attempts of Jewish and heathen powers against the gospel
Uncited in the Gospels and unreferred to Christ until Hebrews; here is the apostles’ own school of interpretation

debates.question: How did the whole company speak one prayer?

sides.position: The people most likely followed Peter clause by clause
Perhaps the company sang the Psalm and Peter then applied it
The phrase means only that they prayed, with one mind and purpose

26.pericope_label: The kings of the earth against the Lord and his Christ: Herod and Pilate with the Gentiles and Israel gathered against thy holy child Jesus

schools.summary: Calvin holds that all who refuse to submit to Christ make war on God, and reads the double-sensed word as either fitting Christ better or alluding to David’s resemblance to him, and explains the two peoples as one body drawn from many countries; Gill identifies the kings and presses the holiness of the one they rose against.

Barnes makes opposition to the Messiah opposition to God, reads the paired nouns as parallelism, and prefers son to child; Ellicott renders the title Servant and notes the missing articles; Lightfoot explains why the Jews would resist the added words in this city; Robertson notes that only this writer records the two rulers’ reconciliation.
Clarke would translate the word as Anointed and thinks the added in this city far more emphatic; Wesley refers the anointing to the kingship of Israel.
Cyril of Jerusalem applies the raging to those who would be friends of the Father apart from the Son, and asks how one who denies the Door can be thought worthy of entrance.

debates.question: Is the word child, son or servant?

sides.position: Not the usual word for the Lord Jesus and unrelated to age; son would be happier
Servant, as the same word is used of David two verses before
Child, from the union of the human nature with the Son — or else servant, as Mediator
Deliberately double, perhaps to mark the resemblance between David and Christ

debates.question: Who are the Gentiles and the peoples?

sides.position: The Romans who crucified him, and the Jews stirred up by their rulers
Both terms, on the Hebrew usage, denote Israel
One body drawn from many countries, gathered to the feast

28.pericope_label: To do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done; and now, Lord, behold their threatenings

schools.summary: Calvin holds that God brings to pass by the wicked what he determined, bridling them so far as is expedient to exercise us, and convicts those who own foreknowledge without ordination; Gill separates their intention from the event; both read the petition as seeking liberty to preach rather than quiet.

Ellicott states the problem of purpose and free agency and denies that any solution is possible, holding both facts without a formula; Barnes collects the historical facts instead of the theory and notes what the petition does not ask; Robertson sees them rising above sight to the Hand that shapes men’s ends, and finds a wholesome lesson in men who had defied the court still praying for courage.

Clarke reads the clause as a parenthesis belonging to Christ, not to the gatherers, since to make their rage the thing determined would be impious and absurd, and turns the threatenings outward as aimed at God; Wesley reduces the counsel to permission.

debates.question: What was foreordained — their act, or what they opposed?

sides.position: Not their act; the clause is a parenthesis about what Christ was to perform, which they gathered to hinder
Their act itself; God brings to pass by the wicked what he has determined, turning their counsels backward
Not their intention but the event, which providence disposed to God’s decree
Only what God permitted, according to his counsel to save mankind by his Son’s sufferings
The question admits no solution; both facts must be held without a formula of reconciliation

debates.question: What does the church ask for?

sides.position: Not safety but freedom from being deterred, since they had resolved to persevere
Liberty to preach rather than a quiet life, which would forsake their calling
That God notice threatenings aimed at himself, not at them
Courage in deed to match brave words already spoken

30.pericope_label: Grant signs and wonders by the name of Jesus; and the place was shaken and they spake the word with boldness

schools.summary: Calvin asks why men who suffered for one miracle should want more daily, and answers from their preference of God’s glory to their own safety; he refuses to rest on the shaking, since the sign was extraordinary while the answered prayer is the perpetual profit set before us; Gill lists what the healings would accomplish.

Barnes notes that the prayer never asks for safety and gives four reasons why the shaking was taken as an answer; Ellicott hears an assonance between healing and the name of Jesus, and reads the sign as Pentecost renewed but deliberately without the tongues; Robertson takes it for an earthquake and notes the prayer’s own words used of the answer.

Clarke frames the petition as an appeal to magnify the crucified Son, and draws from the fresh filling that grace is given for the time being and not in stock for the future; Wesley notes simply that the petition was granted.

debates.question: Why ask for further miracles?

sides.position: Because they valued the declaring of God’s power above their own safety, whatever the adversaries did
As evidence of the truth of their message; they never asked to be preserved from danger
To magnify the Son whom the council had crucified, and to animate the preachers

debates.question: What was the shaking?

sides.position: An earthquake, and by every mark an answer to the prayer
Pentecost renewed, without the tongues that signified a gift given once for all
A mere token of God’s presence; the fruit that follows is the thing to stand on

32.pericope_label: Of one heart and of one soul, having all things common, and with great power the apostles gave witness

schools.summary: Calvin makes faith the thing that knits hearts, notes that wicked men also conspire so that only the faithful’s concord is holy, orders love before beneficence and denies value to a beneficence not rising from the heart, and says they were beloved because beneficent; Gill numbers the believers and glosses the power three ways.
Henry marvels that strangers of different sects and old civil quarrels became intimate, and calls the church’s increase its glory.

Ellicott separates heart from soul on Hebrew usage, insists the community of goods was voluntary and its owners stewards rather than possessors, and refuses to decide whether the grace is God’s or the people’s; Robertson corrects the English construction, limits the community to use rather than possession, and notes the witness continued on the very point for which they were arrested; Barnes rests the power on the preaching of the resurrection and reads the grace as favour won by kindness.

Clarke matches the ancient definition of a friend against one soul in five thousand bodies and holds the grace to be both God’s favour and the people’s; Wesley grounds the community of goods wholly in the love that made it inevitable.

debates.question: What was the community of goods?

sides.position: Voluntary; property was not abolished but held as stewardship under the law of love
Common in use, not in possession
An inevitable consequence of one soul; while the love lasted it could not be otherwise
The outward fruit whose root is inward love, worthless if it does not rise from the heart

debates.question: Whose grace was upon them all?

sides.position: The people’s favour, won largely by their union and liberality
Both at once, since God’s benevolence is never exerted without his beneficence
Undecidable; there are no sufficient data and the question must be left open

34.pericope_label: No man lacked, for possessors of lands sold them and laid the prices at the apostles’ feet

schools.summary: Calvin holds the universal speech indefinite, restricts the selling to what need required, praises the discretion of an unequal distribution, and turns the passage into a rebuke of his own generation; Gill notes the favour such care of the poor won.

Barnes denies that all sold everything and points to Ananias and to the one man named as proof, and notes the office soon grew burdensome; Ellicott marks the repeated action, suggests the sales were an act of faith in the desolation Christ foretold, and pictures the Eastern manner of giving at the feet; Robertson keeps the tenses of selling and distributing in view.

Clarke explains the need from the loss of the poor’s share in the sacrifices and calls the provision temporary; Wesley makes the absence of want the proof of the grace, and holds that the same grace would produce the same effect in any age.

debates.question: Did every believer sell all?

sides.position: No; the phrase is indefinite, and Ananias and the man named prove it was not obligatory
There was no command, but the same grace anywhere would bear the same fruit
It met a temporary need created by the poor’s exclusion from the sacrifices

debates.question: Why sell land in particular?

sides.position: Faith in the coming desolation their Master had foretold, land being then a source of anxiety
They were preparing to leave their native country and preach elsewhere
Because need required it, and the distribution was measured to each case

36.pericope_label: Joses, surnamed Barnabas by the apostles, a Levite of Cyprus, having land, sold it and laid the money at the apostles’ feet

schools.summary: Gill leaves open where the land lay and how it was got, rehearsing the Levitical rule and the rabbinic reading of it, and notes the name is a contraction.

Barnes gives three reasons for the naming and traces the man’s later career with Paul; Robertson infers from the singling out that not all actually sold, and alone doubts that the apostles coined the name; Ellicott derives it as son of prophecy or counsel, reads it as the gift of paraclesis, and supposes an earlier acquaintance behind the later friendship; Lightfoot takes the surname as distinguishing two noted men of one name.

Clarke allows individual Levites to purchase land anywhere, argues the name means son of exhortation, and observes that both apostles to the Gentiles were born in Gentile countries; Wesley refers the title to the fortune given and the gifts exercised.
Chrysostom explains the naming as a deliberate foil: the virtuous deed is set down first so that the sin about to be related may appear at its worst.

debates.question: Why is this man named?

sides.position: As a foil, so that the sin about to be told may show at its worst
Because he was a foreigner, remarkably liberal, and afterwards eminent in the ministry
As one illustration only — which argues that not all in fact sold

debates.question: What does the new name mean?

sides.position: Son of prophecy, rendered by a Greek word for exhortation
Son of prophecy or counsel, marking the gift of persuasive utterance the apostles traced to the Spirit
Encouragement is the chief idea, but the apostles may not have coined the name at all
Both his liberality and his gifts of comfort and exhortation
